title: Generator convoy stuck at an unregulated junction — March 2026
summary: A generator dispatched to a critical hospital was held 16 minutes at a junction with broken signals and no police, while transit times across the whole corridor kept growing behind it. The dispatch decision had been right; the route was never guaranteed.
outcome: A police unit arrived and the convoy completed the last stretch in 6 minutes. Lesson: key junctions must be regulated before the convoy passes — an unregulated junction can cost more than the entire drive.

title: Police pulled from a junction and the corridor seized up — May 2026
summary: The police unit regulating the busiest junction was diverted to a hospital emergency. Within minutes congestion climbed along every route that crossed the junction, delaying three crews that were already en route elsewhere.
outcome: The unit returned 35 minutes later and the corridor recovered. Lesson: lifting regulation from a junction has a cost that shows up minutes later on every route through it — only divert if the new destination outweighs holding the corridor.

title: Congestion trend detected and regulated before the first convoy — July 2026
summary: As the blackout began, congestion at the junction started climbing minutes before any convoy was dispatched. A police unit was sent on the trend alone and the junction was already being directed when the first generator came through.
outcome: No convoy lost time at the junction for the rest of the crisis. Lesson: send police on the congestion trend, not once crews are already blocked — a junction held in advance is cheaper than one unblocked in a hurry.

title: Junction signals failed with no police at all — February 2026
summary: The junction's signals failed with the blackout and no police unit was assigned, so every crew crossing it lost time and three generators arrived late along the corridor.
outcome: A police unit was assigned 18 minutes later. Lesson: a signal failure at a junction needs police before convoys arrive; the junction regulates traffic, not the other way around.

title: Police sent to the wrong junction — April 2026
summary: Two junctions share a similar name and the police unit was sent to the quieter one while the busy junction stayed unregulated and its congestion climbed.
outcome: The unit was redirected 12 minutes late. Lesson: confirm the junction id and its current congestion before assigning police; a unit at the wrong junction regulates nothing that matters.

title: Cascading congestion from a single unregulated junction — June 2026
summary: One unregulated junction slowed a single convoy, which then blocked the next one, and congestion spread across the district's routes within minutes.
outcome: Every crew's ETA slipped and a hospital generator arrived late. Lesson: treat the first convoy delay at a junction as the start of a cascade; regulate the junction before the queue reaches the next route.

title: High congestion at the junction was ignored as noise — August 2026
summary: The junction's congestion climbed steadily but stayed below the alarm threshold, so no police were sent until convoys were already blocked.
outcome: Three resources lost 15 minutes each. Lesson: watch the congestion trend at a key junction, not only the alarm threshold; a junction at 80% of the threshold is already costing time.

title: Police diverted from the junction to a hospital — October 2026
summary: The police unit holding the main junction was pulled to a hospital emergency and the corridor congested within minutes, delaying every crew that used it.
outcome: The unit returned 30 minutes later and the corridor recovered. Lesson: lifting regulation from a junction costs every route through it; divert the unit only when the new destination outweighs the corridor delay.

title: Stalled vehicles blocked the lanes near the junction — December 2026
summary: Several vehicles stalled in the blackout and blocked the lanes approaching the junction, so even with directions the convoys could not pass.
outcome: A tow crew cleared the lanes after 16 minutes. Lesson: when congestion is caused by stalled vehicles, send clearing resources, not only police; directing traffic around a blocked lane does not open it.

title: Faulty congestion reading hid a blocked junction — January 2026
summary: A faulty congestion sensor reported light traffic while the junction was actually gridlocked, so no police were dispatched until crews reported being stuck.
outcome: The units arrived 14 minutes late. Lesson: cross-check a low congestion reading against crew reports; a faulty sensor can hide a junction that has already seized up.

title: Preventive regulation on a congestion trend — March 2026
summary: The junction's congestion began rising minutes before any convoy was dispatched, and a police unit was sent on the trend alone.
outcome: The junction was already being directed when the first convoy arrived. Lesson: regulate on a congestion trend, not once crews are blocked; a junction held early costs less than one unblocked in a hurry.

title: Two junctions failed and only one police unit existed — May 2026
summary: Two junctions lost their signals at once and only one police unit was available. It was assigned to the junction with more routes crossing it.
outcome: The other junction delayed local traffic but the main corridor stayed open. Lesson: with one police unit and two failed junctions, regulate the one carrying more routes and hold the other with signed diversions.
